name: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg)
summary: HBsAg is a protein on the surface of the hepatitis B virus (HBV); its presence in blood is the primary marker of a current HBV infection, whether acute or chronic. It is typically the first serologic marker to appear after exposure.
whatItMeans: A non-reactive (negative) result means no HBsAg was detected, so current active HBV infection is unlikely. A reactive (positive) result indicates a current infection and that the person is considered infectious; it does not, by itself, distinguish acute from chronic disease, so it should be confirmed and interpreted alongside the full HBV panel (anti-HBs, total and IgM anti-HBc, and often HBV DNA). HBsAg persisting for more than 6 months generally indicates chronic infection. Note that HBsAg reflects active infection, not immunity — immunity from vaccination or resolved infection is shown by anti-HBs (surface antibody), not HBsAg. This is educational information, not a diagnosis; results should be reviewed with a clinician.
confounders: Recent HBV vaccination (transient HBsAg positivity, typically within ~30 days of a dose)
Window period (early after exposure HBsAg may not yet be detectable)
Assay differences and rare false positives/negatives requiring confirmatory testing
